title: 6 holiday side hustles to start under $200
description: Six legit holiday side hustles with checked starter costs, what customers pay pros, and how to land your first 3 clients before the rush.
image_alt: Infographic: 6 holiday side hustles to start under $200: light hanging ~$150, snow clearing ~$60, window washing ~$50, gift wrapping ~$30, leaf cleanup ~$180, car interiors ~$150.
intro: From mid-November to early January, people run out of time before they run out of to-dos. Lights need hanging, driveways need clearing, gifts need wrapping and the car needs to look decent before the family visits. That's work you can get paid for, and none of it needs a big investment.

Below are the six ideas from our post, with the starter kit we priced on real store pages, what customers typically pay professionals, and the simplest way to land your first three customers. Start with one; add a second when the first is booked out.

ideas.name: Light Hanging
ideas.what: You hang the customer's outdoor holiday lights along gutters, rooflines, windows and bushes, then come back in January to take them down. Most of the job is planning the layout, safe ladder work and neat clipping.
ideas.who: you're comfortable on a ladder, like tidy detail work and can work a few evenings and weekends in November.
ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$150 total is the ladder plus a pack of clips. Customers usually supply their own lights; if you supply them, charge for them separately.

charge.text: Professional holiday light installation averages **$240–$650 installed**, or about **$2.50–$5.00 per foot** including lights.

first_customers: Hang your own (or a friend's) lights first and take clear before/after photos at dusk.
Post those photos in your neighborhood Facebook group or on Nextdoor with a simple offer: install now, take-down in January included.
Knock on doors of one-story homes on your street, especially older neighbors who shouldn't be on ladders.
ideas.watch_out: stick to one-story rooflines until you're experienced, always have someone hold the ladder on uneven ground, and never staple or nail through gutters or shingles. Only plug lights into outdoor-rated outlets; leave any electrical wiring work to licensed electricians.

ideas.name: Snow Clearing
ideas.first_job: A neighbor's driveway after the first storm
ideas.what: You shovel driveways, walkways and steps after snowfall and spread ice melt on slippery spots. Customers value reliability most: being there before they need to leave for work.
ideas.who: you live where it snows, you're fine with early mornings and physical work, and your customers are within walking distance.
ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$60 total is the ice melt plus a basic combo shovel.

charge.text: Shoveling an average driveway typically costs **$30–$70 per visit**; seasonal contracts average **$200–$600 per season**.

first_customers: Make a "storm list" before the first snow: ask neighbors if they want you to come automatically after every snowfall.
Offer a simple per-visit price and a discounted season price, paid up front.
Start with seniors and busy parents on your street; one reliable season usually means they book you again next year.
ideas.watch_out: shoveling heavy snow is hard on your back and heart. Lift small loads, push instead of lifting where you can and take breaks. Ask before using ice melt near plants, pets or new concrete.

ideas.name: Window Washing
ideas.first_job: Ground-floor and inside windows before a holiday party
ideas.what: You clean glass, frames and sills, inside and out, so homes look their best before guests arrive. A good squeegee technique is most of the skill and takes an afternoon of practice.
ideas.who: you like quick, visible results and want something you can do year-round, not just in December.

kit.item: Unger Total Pro window cleaning kit (squeegee, scrubber, pole)
kit.amazon: window cleaning kit squeegee extension pole

charge.text: Residential window cleaning averages **$220 per visit**, with a typical range of **$150–$302**, or about **$4–$8 per window**.

first_customers: Practice on your own windows until there are no streaks, then photograph a before/after pane in good light.
Offer a "party-ready" package for the weeks before Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Leave a short flyer with a per-window price at homes with lots of front-facing glass.
ideas.watch_out: start with ground-floor and interior windows only; second-story work on ladders is where injuries happen. On freezing days, stick to interior glass.

ideas.name: Gift Wrapping
ideas.first_job: A busy friend's or coworker's gift pile
ideas.what: You wrap gifts beautifully for busy people and small shops. You can work from home with drop-off, go to customers' homes, or set up a table at a local shop or holiday market.
ideas.who: you're neat, patient and creative, and want a low-cost idea you can do indoors. This is also one of the easiest ideas for teens.
ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$30 total is paper plus tape and ribbon to start. Buy more as orders come in.

charge.text: On Taskrabbit, gift wrapping services average **about $20 per hour**, varying by location and job size.

first_customers: Wrap 5 gifts with different styles and photograph them as your menu.
Ask a local boutique if you can wrap at a table on busy weekends (they get happy customers, you get the jobs).
Offer office drop-off: collect gifts at a workplace on Monday, return them wrapped on Wednesday.
ideas.watch_out: agree on paper and price before you start, and charge more for oversized or oddly shaped items. Keep a simple list of whose gifts are whose so nothing gets mixed up.

ideas.name: Leaf Cleanup
ideas.first_job: A corner lot after the big leaf drop
ideas.what: You blow, rake and bag leaves from lawns, beds and driveways, then leave them where your town collects yard waste. It's peak season right now in most of the country.
ideas.who: you like outdoor work, have weekends free and live in an area with lots of trees.

kit.item: Ryobi 40V cordless leaf blower kit (battery + charger)
kit.amazon: cordless leaf blower with battery and charger

charge.text: Leaf removal averages **$376**, with most homeowners paying **$190–$591**; hourly rates run about **$15–$60** depending on raking, blowing or vacuuming.

first_customers: Walk your neighborhood the weekend after a windy day and note the yards that are buried.
Leave a simple door hanger: one-time cleanup price plus an optional second visit in December.
Ask your first customers' neighbors; matching yards on one street saves you travel time.
ideas.watch_out: check your town's yard-waste rules (bags vs curb piles, pickup dates) and any leaf-blower hour limits before you start. Wear eye and hearing protection.

ideas.name: Car Interiors
ideas.first_job: A family car before holiday road trips
ideas.what: You vacuum, wipe down and refresh car interiors: seats, mats, cup holders, door panels and windows. Holiday travel and visiting family make December a busy month.
ideas.who: you're detail-oriented and can work at customers' driveways or have space at home.

kit.item: Microfiber cloths and interior cleaner spray

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$150 total is the shop vac plus cloths and an interior spray.

charge.text: Car interior detailing typically costs **$150–$350**; a basic interior clean is about **$150–$200**.

first_customers: Detail your own or a friend's car and take before/after photos of the worst spots (floor mats and cup holders sell it).
Offer a "road trip ready" interior package in the two weeks before Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Ask parents at school pickup or sports practice; family cars need it most.
ideas.watch_out: test any cleaner on a hidden spot first and don't promise to remove every stain. Ask before plugging into a customer's outlet, and remove valuables with the owner present.

getting_started: **Check local rules.** Search "[your city] business license" to see whether you need one. Some cities require a general business license even for small side work.
**Think about insurance.** Ask a local agent about general liability insurance before ladder or yard work; a single accident can cost more than a season's income.
**Set clear prices.** Write a simple price list (per visit, per window, per gift) and give written quotes by text so there are no surprises.
**Take payment simply.** Use a payment app you already have and send a receipt for every job.
**Track every dollar.** Keep receipts for tools and supplies; side income is taxable, so set some aside.
tip: Ask every happy client for **one neighbor's name**. That's your next job.

faq.q: Which of these is cheapest to start?
faq.a: Gift wrapping, at about $30 for paper, tape and ribbon. Window washing is next at about $50.

faq.q: Do I need a business license?
faq.a: It depends on your city and state. Many places require a general business license for paid services, even part-time. Search your city's website or call the clerk's office before you start.

We don't promise earnings. The ranges above are what customers typically pay professionals, from published cost guides. As a beginner, expect to charge less until you have reviews and photos of your work.
Gift wrapping, window washing (ground floor) and leaf cleanup are good starter jobs for teens with a parent's OK. Skip ladder work and check your state's rules for working minors.

faq.q: What if it doesn't snow where I live?
faq.a: Swap snow clearing for leaf cleanup or window washing. Both work in milder climates and keep going after the holidays.
